messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tax Consultant
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Conflict: Confrontations, Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others, Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ethan McCall is a 36-year-old married North American man who came to treatment after several months of feeling increasingly unable to settle into ordinary life, even in settings that had once felt predictable and safe. Before the trauma, he had worked steadily as a tax consultant, a role that suited his preference for structure, careful attention, and long stretches of focused work. That order was shattered during his military deployment, when a confrontation around him escalated into sudden danger and left him with a violent experience he still struggled to describe in full. In his telling, the details arrive in fragments: the pressure of panic, the sense that the situation could turn without warning, and one vivid sensory trace that still catches him off guard—the taste he remembers from that moment, which can return so clearly in his mouth that it feels as though the event has come back into the room with him.

In the early weeks afterward, Ethan tried to carry on as if nothing had changed, but he found that certain conversation topics would pull him back into the event with startling force. Any discussion that drifted toward combat, violence, or other aspects of what had happened made him tense and silent, and he learned to steer away from those exchanges before anyone could ask too much. He also began to avoid talking about the event or its aftermath altogether, even with people he trusted. When his wife or a close friend tried to check in, he would give short answers or change the subject, saying he did not want to “open it up” again. He had come to believe that speaking about it would make the feelings flood back too intensely, and he preferred to keep the experience sealed away rather than risk being overwhelmed.

That overwhelm has been a defining feature of his recollections. Ethan described moments when the memory returns without warning and the emotion becomes so intense that he has to stop whatever he is doing. At other times, the same memory comes back in a strange, flattened way, and he can recall what happened while feeling completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger. He said this contrast unsettles him almost as much as the memory itself, because he never knows whether he will be flooded by feeling or left oddly detached. What frightened him most was that both states could arrive suddenly and leave him disoriented.

Over time, his sense of safety in the present narrowed. He became highly alert to touch, reacting with alarm when someone touches him unexpectedly. At home, this has created awkward moments with his wife, who has learned to announce herself before reaching for him, especially if he is deep in concentration or already tense. Ethan does not experience this as a personal slight; rather, he explains it as his body going on guard before his mind can catch up. He also finds unusual silence deeply unsettling. In quiet rooms, at a pause in conversation, or in a still hallway, he can feel that something dangerous is about to happen. At work, this has become particularly noticeable in the calm stretches of his day. As a tax consultant, he often sits in a quiet office reviewing documents or speaking in low tones with clients, and those silent intervals can make him scan the room and listen for what might come next. Before he feels comfortable anywhere, he always identifies escape routes, mentally noting doors, exits, and the quickest way out. Even in restaurants or waiting areas, he positions himself with this in mind, a habit that has become as automatic as reading an intake form or checking a calculation.

He has also altered how he lets himself respond emotionally. Moments of warmth, relief, or pleasure now make him uneasy, and he pushes away positive feelings because they feel unsafe to him, as though allowing himself to settle would leave him exposed. He described this as keeping one hand on the brake even when things are going well. Physical closeness has become another source of discomfort. He avoids being touched in any form, including casual contact from family or colleagues, and his wife has had to adapt to a marriage that now includes careful spacing and deliberate warning before any affectionate gesture. The changes have not gone unnoticed in the household, and Ethan is aware that his withdrawal has made him harder to reach, even though he is not trying to be rejecting.

He sought help after realizing that these patterns had begun to shape nearly every part of his day. The work that once gave him stability now feels threaded with scanning, bracing, and quiet avoidance, and he is tired of organizing his life around exits, silence, and the possibility of being startled. He came in hoping to understand why his body still reacts as though danger is close, and he is most afraid that he will remain cut off from both his wife and the ordinary ease he used to take for granted. At the same time, he is hoping for a way to talk about what happened without being flooded or going numb, and for a future in which being touched, being quiet, or being at peace no longer feels like something he has to defend against.
